caption_hook: North Dakota hides glacier rubble, dinosaur bones and an oil-rich shale two miles down.

layers.name: COLEHARBOR GROUP
layers.hook: Left behind by the ice sheets
layers.what: Ice-age glaciers bulldozed across the state and dumped a blanket of clay, sand and boulders. Meltwater lakes added flat silt beds, like the old Lake Agassiz floor around Fargo.
layers.bonus: Devils Lake has no natural outlet, so it keeps rising and falling with the rain.

layers.name: SENTINEL BUTTE FM.
layers.hook: Swamps, coal and a painted canyon
layers.what: Warm, wet forests once covered western North Dakota. Their mud and coal built the banded buttes of Theodore Roosevelt National Park, where petrified wood weathers out.
layers.bonus: Burning coal seams baked the clay into red scoria, now used to surface local roads.

layers.name: HELL CREEK FORMATION
layers.what: River floodplains where Triceratops and T. rex roamed in the final years of the dinosaurs. The top of the formation records the asteroid impact that ended their reign.
layers.bonus: Near Marmarth you can see the thin boundary layer from the extinction itself.

layers.name: BAKKEN FORMATION
layers.hook: The shale that sparked an oil rush
layers.what: A black, oil-rich shale laid down in a warm sea, now buried about two miles deep in the Williston Basin. Horizontal drilling and fracking unlocked it in the 2000s.
layers.bonus: It is named for Henry Bakken, whose farm near Tioga was drilled in 1951.

layers.name: THE BASEMENT
layers.what: Beneath every layer lies old crystalline rock, the roots of an ancient continent. None of it reaches the surface in North Dakota; we know it only from deep drill holes.
layers.bonus: The Williston Basin sagged so slowly that it kept collecting layers for hundreds of millions of years.
